lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server instance named SQL1 that hosts five databases.  
  
You need to migrate the databases to an Azure SQL managed instance. The solution must:  
  
- Minimize downtime  
- Prevent data loss  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
Log shipping (and its Azure-native implementation, the Log Replay Service) continuously copies and restores full, differential, and transaction log backups from the on-premises SQL Server to the target Azure SQL Managed Instance. Because the databases stay in a restoring state and are kept current via ongoing log backups, the final cutover only requires restoring the last (tail-log) backup, which minimizes the downtime window and ensures no committed transactions are lost. Backup and Restore requires a single offline backup/restore operation that causes extended downtime and risks losing transactions committed after the backup is taken; Data Migration Assistant only assesses compatibility and migrates schema, not live data with minimal downtime; and Always On availability groups are not a supported direct migration mechanism from on-premises SQL Server to Azure SQL Managed Instance in this generic form.

**Learn more:** [Migrate SQL Server Databases by Using Log Replay Service - Azure SQL Managed Instance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/managed-instance/log-replay-service-migrate?view=azuresql) · [SQL Server to Azure SQL Managed Instance: Migration Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/data-migration/sql-server/managed-instance/guide)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL database named DB1 that includes a nonclustered index named index1.  
  
End users report slow queries when using index1.  
  
You need to identify the operations being performed on the index.  
  
Which dynamic management view should you use?
questions.explanation:
To identify the actual operations being performed on an index, use sys.dm_db_index_operational_stats, which returns current low-level I/O, locking, latching, and access-method activity per index (for example range_scan_count, singleton_lookup_count, leaf/nonleaf insert/update/delete counts, and page-latch/lock waits). This is what reveals contention and access patterns behind slow queries on index1. sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats (choice D, also misspelled) only reports how many query plans used the index (seeks/scans/lookups/updates counts) rather than the operations and waits occurring on it, and physical_stats reports fragmentation. Hence the operational_stats DMV is correct.

**Learn more:** [sys.dm_db_index_operational_stats](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/system-dynamic-management-views/sys-dm-db-index-operational-stats-transact-sql) · [sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/system-dynamic-management-views/sys-dm-db-index-usage-stats-transact-sql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL Database elastic pool that includes 10 databases.  
  
You receive the following alert:  
  
```text  
Msg 1132, Level 16, state 1, Line 1  
The elastic pool has reached its storage limit. The storage used for the elastic pool cannot exceed (76800) MBs.  
```  
  
You need to resolve the alert while minimizing administrative effort.  
  
Which three actions can you take? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Increase the maximum storage of the elastic pool.
Remove a database from the pool.

questions.explanation:
Elastic-pool storage is shared by its databases. The limit can be resolved by increasing the pool’s maximum storage, moving a database outside the pool so its storage is no longer shared there, or shrinking a database to reclaim unused allocated file space. Deleting rows alone does not automatically reclaim allocated file space; compression is not a guaranteed complete remedy for the pool-level storage limit.

**Learn more:** [Manage file space for databases in Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/file-space-manage?view=azuresql-db) · [Resource management in dense elastic pools](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/elastic-pool-resource-management?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL database named DB1.  
  
You have a table named Table1 that contains 20 columns of type CHAR(400). Row compression is enabled for Table1.  
  
During a database audit, you find that none of the fields contains more than 150 characters.  
  
You need to ensure that page compression can be applied to Table1.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Change the column type to NVARCHAR(MAX).
Change the column type to VARCHAR(MAX).
Change the column type to VARCHAR(200).

questions.explanation:
A table cannot be enabled for row or page compression when its maximum row size plus compression overhead exceeds 8,060 bytes. Changing the 20 fixed-length CHAR(400) columns to VARCHAR(200) lowers the maximum declared row width sufficiently while still accommodating values of up to 150 characters. Sparse columns cannot be used with data compression, and off-row data is not compressed.

**Learn more:** [Data compression - SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/data-compression/data-compression?view=sql-server-ver17) · [Page and Extent Architecture Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/pages-and-extents-architecture-guide?view=sql-server-ver17)

You need to create an implementation plan for configuring data retention on ResearchDB1. The solution must satisfy the security and compliance requirements.  
  
What should the plan include?

options.text: Configure the Deleted databases settings for ResearchSrv01.
Deploy and configure an Azure Backup server.
Configure the Advanced Data Security settings for ResearchDB1.
Configure the Manage Backups settings for ResearchSrv01.

questions.explanation:
Long-term retention (LTR) for Azure SQL Database backups is configured through the 'Manage Backups' settings at the logical SQL server level (ResearchSrv01). This feature allows administrators to define retention policies that keep full database backups for extended periods (up to 10 years) to satisfy compliance and regulatory requirements. The 'Deleted databases' setting only helps recover accidentally deleted databases within the standard retention window and does not provide configurable long-term retention. 'Advanced Data Security' addresses threat detection, vulnerability assessment, and data classification, not backup retention. Deploying an Azure Backup server applies to hybrid or VM-based backup scenarios, not to native Azure SQL Database backup management.

**Learn more:** [Configure long-term backup retention - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/long-term-retention-configure)

Which statement should you run?

options.text: BACKUP DATABASE DB1 TO URL='https://mystorageaccount.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/DB1.bak' with (Differential, STATS=5, COMPRESSION);

You need to implement a solution to notify the administrators, and this solution must satisfy the monitoring requirements.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create an Azure Monitor alert rule that has a static threshold and assign the alert rule to an action group.
Add a diagnostic setting that logs QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics and streams to an Azure event hub.
Add a diagnostic setting that logs Timeouts and streams to an Azure event hub.
Create an Azure Monitor alert rule that has a dynamic threshold and assign the alert rule to an action group.

questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor dynamic threshold alert rules use machine learning to learn a metric's historical behavior (including hourly, daily, and weekly seasonal patterns) and automatically calculate appropriate upper and lower bounds, firing when the metric deviates from its normal, expected pattern — such as a database showing higher-than-average CPU usage. Assigning the alert rule to an action group is what triggers the actual notification (for example, an email) to the administrators. Diagnostic settings that stream QueryStoreRuntimeStatistics or Timeouts logs to an Event Hub only forward telemetry data for storage or downstream analysis and do not generate administrator notifications on their own, and a static threshold would require a manually fixed value that does not account for normal variability in the metric over time.

**Learn more:** [Create a Log Search alert rule with dynamic threshold - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-dynamic-thresholds) · [Configure streaming export of metrics and resource logs - Azure SQL Database & Azure SQL Managed Instance | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/metrics-diagnostic-telemetry-logging-streaming-export-configure?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a SQL pool in Azure Synapse that includes a table named `dbo.Customers`. The table has a column named `Email`.  
  
You need to stop nonadministrative users from viewing complete email addresses in the `Email` column. Instead, users must see values in the format `[email protected]`.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: From the Azure portal, set a mask on the Email column.
From the Azure portal, set a sensitivity classification of Confidential for the Email column.
From Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio, set an email mask on the Email column.
From Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio, grant the SELECT permission to the users for all the columns in the dbo.Customers table except Email.

questions.explanation:
Dynamic data masking hides sensitive values in query results for nonprivileged users while retaining the original values in the database. An email mask exposes only a limited email-style value, such as `aXX@XXXX.com`. Azure Synapse Analytics supports dynamic data masking for dedicated SQL pools; configuring the mask with T-SQL through SQL Server Management Studio satisfies this requirement. Sensitivity classification does not mask returned data, and column-level SELECT denial prevents access instead of returning a masked value.

**Learn more:** [Dynamic Data Masking - Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/dynamic-data-masking-overview?view=azuresql) · [T-SQL feature support in Azure Synapse SQL pools](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/synapse-analytics/sql/overview-features)

This capability operates on the lightweight query execution statistics profiling infrastructure. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises datacenter that hosts a 2-TB Microsoft SQL Server 2019 database named DB1.  
  
You need to recommend a solution to migrate DB1 to an Azure SQL managed instance. The solution must minimize downtime and administrative effort.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?
questions.explanation:
Log Replay Service (LRS) is the managed migration service for moving SQL Server databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to design a data retention solution for the Twitter feed data records. The solution must meet the customer sentiment analytics requirements.  
  
Which Azure Storage functionality should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
Azure Storage lifecycle management policies let you define rule-based, automated actions on blob data based on its age (e.g., delete blobs after a specified number of days since creation or last modification). This capability directly supports a retention requirement that mandates automatically purging Twitter feed data records after a defined period, without needing custom application code. In contrast, time-based retention and soft delete are data-protection features that prevent or allow recovery of deletions/modifications for compliance purposes, and change feed simply logs changes to blobs for auditing or replication scenarios — none of which implement automated, age-based data purging required for the retention solution.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that uses a domain named contoso.com.  
  
You have two Azure VMs named DBServer1 and DBServer2, each hosting a default SQL Server instance. DBServer1 is located in the East US Azure region and contains a database named DatabaseA. DBServer2 is located in the West US Azure region.  
  
DBServer1 experiences a high volume of data changes and has low-latency requirements for data writes.  
  
You need to configure a new availability group for DatabaseA, with the secondary replica residing on DBServer2.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the primary endpoint as TCP://DBServer1.contoso.com:445, configure the secondary endpoint as TCP://DBServer2.contoso.com:445, and set the availability mode to Asynchronous.
Configure the primary endpoint as TCP://DBServer1.contoso.com:445, configure the secondary endpoint as TCP://DBServer2.contoso.com:445, and set the availability mode to Synchronous.
Configure the primary endpoint as TCP://DBServer1.contoso.com:5022, configure the secondary endpoint as TCP://DBServer2.contoso.com:5022, and set the availability mode to Asynchronous.
Configure the primary endpoint as TCP://DBServer1.contoso.com:5022, configure the secondary endpoint as TCP://DBServer2.contoso.com:5022, and set the availability mode to Synchronous.

questions.explanation:
SQL Server Always On Availability Group (database mirroring) endpoints listen on TCP port 5022 by default, not 445, so the endpoint must be configured as TCP://DBServer1.contoso.com:5022 and TCP://DBServer2.contoso.com:5022. Because DBServer1 and DBServer2 are in different, geographically distant Azure regions (East US and West US), the network latency between them is too high to support synchronous-commit mode without degrading write performance, since synchronous-commit requires the primary to wait for the secondary to harden the log before committing. Given DatabaseA's high volume of changes and low write-latency requirement, the availability mode should be set to Asynchronous, which lets the primary commit transactions without waiting on the secondary.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Always On Availability Groups Configuration (SQL Server)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/availability-groups/windows/troubleshoot-always-on-availability-groups-configuration-sql-server?view=sql-server-ver17) · [Availability group database mirroring endpoint - PowerShell](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/availability-groups/windows/database-mirroring-always-on-availability-groups-powershell?view=sql-server-ver16)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have several Azure SQL databases on the same Azure SQL Database server in a resource group called ResourceGroup1.  
  
You must receive an alert when CPU utilization exceeds 80 percent for any database. The solution must apply to any additional databases created on the Azure SQL server.  
  
Which resource type should you use to create the alert?
questions.explanation:
To alert on CPU exceeding 80% for any database, including databases created later, you create the Azure Monitor metric alert scoped at the logical SQL server (resource type SQL servers / Microsoft.Sql/servers) rather than at each individual database. A server-scoped alert automatically evaluates all current and future databases on that server, satisfying the requirement to cover additional databases without creating new rules. Scoping to the resource group (choice A) would include unrelated resource types and would not cleanly target the databases' cpu_percent metric, and SQL Databases would have to be re-created per new database. So the correct resource type is SQL Servers.

You have an Azure SQL database called DB1.  
  
You must ensure that DB1 supports automatic failover with no data loss if a datacenter fails, while minimizing costs.  
  
Which deployment option and pricing tier should you configure?

options.text: Azure SQL Database managed instance General Purpose

questions.explanation:
Zone-redundant Azure SQL Database Premium places existing high-availability replicas in separate availability zones. Azure automatically promotes a synchronized replica when a datacenter or zone fails, with no expected data loss. Enabling zone redundancy for the Premium tier does not add cost because it uses the tier’s existing replicas.\
\
**Learn more:** [Reliability in Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/reliability-sql-database)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises datacenter containing a 14-TB Microsoft SQL Server database.  
  
You plan to create an Azure SQL Managed Instance and migrate the on-premises database to that new instance.  
  
Which three service tiers support the SQL Managed Instance? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.  
  
> **NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
A 14-TB database on Azure SQL Managed Instance needs a tier/hardware combination that reserves at least 14 TB of instance storage. General Purpose (both standard-series and premium-series) supports up to 16 TB (32 TB on next-gen), so General Purpose Standard (A) and General Purpose Premium (C) both qualify. On Business Critical, the memory optimized premium-series reaches 16 TB at 64+ vCores without a regional cap (B), whereas Business Critical premium-series only reaches 16 TB in select major regions and is otherwise limited to 5.5 TB, and Business Critical standard-series maxes out at 4 TB (E) - too small. The three tiers that reliably support 14 TB are therefore General Purpose Standard, Business Critical Memory Optimized Premium, and General Purpose Premium.

**Learn more:** [SQL Managed Instance resource limits](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/managed-instance/resource-limits?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have SQL Server 2019 running on an Azure virtual machine with Windows Server 2019. The virtual machine has 4 vCPUs and 28 GB of memory.  
  
You scale up the virtual machine to 8 vCPUs and 64 GB of memory.  
  
You need to reduce tempdb contention without adversely affecting server performance.  
  
How many secondary data files should you configure for tempdb?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft's guidance to reduce tempdb allocation (PFS/GAM/SGAM) contention is: if the number of logical processors is eight or fewer, use the same number of tempdb data files as logical processors, up to a maximum of eight. After scaling the VM to 8 vCPUs, the recommended configuration is 8 tempdb data files, which balances contention reduction against overhead (going far beyond 8, such as 64 files, would add overhead without benefit). Given the answer options, 8 is the correct value. Existing answer B (4) reflects the pre-scale core count, not the post-scale 8-vCPU target.

**Learn more:** [Recommendations to reduce allocation contention](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/sql/database-engine/performance/recommendations-reduce-allocation-contention)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL database named db1 on a server called server1.

What should you do?

options.text: Connect to db1 and run the sp_configure command.
Connect to the master database of server1 and run the sp_configure command.

questions.explanation:
In Azure SQL Database, MAXDOP is a database-scoped configuration. It is changed for the target database by using `ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP = ...`; therefore, modifying db1's database scoped configuration is required.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine.

options.text: Attach a stripe set that contains four 1-TB SSDs.
Attach a RAID-5 array that contains five 1-TB SSDs.

questions.explanation:
Striping multiple Premium SSDs aggregates their individual IOPS and throughput limits into one volume. Four 1-TB disks provide the required 4-TB capacity while maximizing available IOPS, subject to the virtual machine's disk-performance limits. RAID-5 parity processing and mirroring do not provide the same IOPS-maximizing striped configuration.

options.text: The table contains less than 10,000 rows.

questions.explanation:
Data skew means rows are not distributed evenly across the 60 distributions. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL database called DB1.  
  
You must ensure that DB1 supports automatic failover with no data loss if a datacenter fails. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
Which deployment option and pricing tier should you configure?
questions.explanation:
A zone-redundant Azure SQL Database deployment replicates committed data synchronously across availability zones and automatically fails over during a datacenter or zone outage with no expected data loss. The Premium tier supports zone redundancy, and its existing replicas can be distributed across zones without an additional zone-redundancy charge. Basic does not support zone redundancy; General Purpose serverless has an extra charge for it; and Hyperscale is unnecessary for this requirement.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An Azure SQL managed instance named SQLMI1 hosts 10 databases.  
  
You need to implement alerts using Azure Monitor. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Minimize costs.  
- Aggregate Intelligent Insights telemetry from every database.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: From the Diagnostic settings of each database, select Send to Log Analytics.
From the Diagnostic settings of each database, select Stream to an event hub.
From the Diagnostic settings of SQLMI1, select Send to Log Analytics.
From the Diagnostic settings of SQLMI1, select Stream to an event hub.

questions.explanation:
For Azure SQL Managed Instance, Intelligent Insights is the `SQLInsights` diagnostic log at the individual instance-database scope; the managed-instance resource has separate telemetry. Configure diagnostic settings on each database and send `SQLInsights` directly to a shared Log Analytics workspace, where Azure Monitor log alerts can query the aggregated data. This avoids Event Hubs costs and an unnecessary forwarding path.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy two SQL Server instances on Azure virtual machines in a highly available configuration that uses an Always On availability group.  
  
You need to recommend a deployment solution that meets these requirements:  
  
- Provides a Service Level Agreement (SLA) of at least 99.95%  
- Replicates databases within the same group synchronously  
- Minimizes database-write latency  
  
What should you recommend?

options.text: Create two proximity groups and two availability sets. Deploy each virtual machine to a unique availability set. Add one virtual machine to each proximity group.
Create a proximity group and an availability set. Deploy each virtual machine to the availability set. Add both virtual machines to the proximity group.
Create a proximity group and two availability sets. Deploy each virtual machine to a unique availability set. Add both virtual machines to the proximity group.
Create two proximity groups and a single availability set. Deploy both virtual machines to the availability set. Add one virtual machine to each proximity group.

questions.explanation:
An availability set containing two or more virtual machines provides the 99.95% Azure VM SLA by distributing the VMs across fault and update domains. A proximity placement group places the compute resources physically close together, minimizing inter-VM latency for synchronous database replication and writes. When VMs belong to an availability set, the proximity placement group should be assigned to the availability set, placing both VMs in the same group.

**Learn more:** [Availability sets overview - Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/availability-set-overview) · [Proximity placement groups - Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/co-location)

Solution: You deploy an Azure SQL database using the Business Critical service tier and Availability Zones.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
The Business Critical tier includes a primary read-write replica and one or more read-only secondary replicas. Zone redundancy distributes those replicas across Availability Zones and enables failover to a replica in another zone if a datacenter or zone fails.\
\
**Learn more:** [Read Queries on Replicas - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/read-scale-out?view=azuresql) · [Reliability in Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/reliability-sql-database)

questions.question:
Solution: You deploy an Azure SQL database that uses the General Purpose service tier and failover groups.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Database failover groups provide a readable geo-secondary through the read-only listener while the primary remains available for read-write access. They support cross-region failover and redirect listener endpoints to the new primary and secondary after a failure. A General Purpose database can participate in a failover group with a matching geo-secondary.\
\
**Learn more:** [Reliability in Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/reliability-sql-database) · [Failover groups overview and best practices - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/failover-group-sql-db?view=azuresql)

Solution: You deploy an Azure SQL Database that uses the General Purpose service tier and geo-replication.  
  
Does this fulfill the goal?
questions.explanation:
Active geo-replication maintains a continuously synchronized, readable secondary database in a separate region. The primary and secondary provide two readable copies during normal operations, and the secondary can be geo-failed over to restore availability after a datacenter failure.\
\
**Learn more:** [Active geo-replication - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/active-geo-replication-overview?view=azuresql) · [Reliability in Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/reliability-sql-database)

You have an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server that uses the FileTables and FILESTREAM features.  
  
You plan to migrate it to Azure SQL.  
  
Which service should you use?

options.text: SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine

questions.explanation:
FILESTREAM and FileTable are unsupported in Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance. SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine preserves the SQL Server environment required to support these features.\

questions.question:
You have an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server that uses the FileTables and FILESTREAM features.  
  
You plan to migrate it to Azure SQL.  
  
Which service should you use?
questions.explanation:
Auto-failover groups build on active geo-replication and manage replication and failover to another Azure region. Their read-write listener endpoint remains unchanged and automatically routes connections to the current primary after failover, reducing application recovery time and operational administration. They can also use a Microsoft-managed failover policy.

A Transact-SQL statement is created to perform index maintenance on a database. It must be scheduled to run once per day against every database by using Transact-SQL commands.  
  
What should be used to schedule the statement?
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Database elastic jobs can schedule recurring execution of Transact-SQL scripts across one or many target databases, including maintenance tasks. Target groups define the databases, and elastic-job schedules support daily recurrence.\

You are designing a star schema for a dataset containing online-order records. Each record has an order date, an order due date, and an order ship date.  
  
You need to ensure that the design delivers the fastest query times when querying records across arbitrary date ranges and aggregating by fiscal calendar attributes.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Create a date dimension table that has a DateTime key.
Create a date dimension table that has an integer key in the format of YYYYMMDD.
Use built-in SQL functions to extract date attributes.
Use integer columns for the date fields.
Use DateTime columns for the date fields.

questions.explanation:
A date dimension with an `int` surrogate key in `YYYYMMDD` format is efficient, sorts numerically, and can contain fiscal-year and fiscal-quarter attributes for aggregation. The order-date, due-date, and ship-date fields in the fact table should be integer foreign keys using that same date key, allowing efficient joins and date-range filtering.

**Learn more:** [Modeling Dimension Tables in Warehouse](https://learn.microsoft.com/bg-bg/fabric//data-warehouse/dimensional-modeling-dimension-tables) · [Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/guidance/star-schema)

After extended periods of inactivity, App1 encounters transient connection errors and timeouts when it tries to access db1.  
  
You need to change db1 to resolve the issues App1 experiences as quickly as possible, without considering immediate costs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Increase the number of vCores allocated to db1.
Decrease the auto-pause delay for db1.

questions.explanation:
An Azure SQL Database in the serverless tier can automatically pause after inactivity. The first connection after a pause initiates auto-resume and can return a database-unavailable error or time out until the database is online. Disabling auto-pause keeps the database available, removing the pause/resume delay; immediate cost is not a constraint.

**Learn more:** [Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/serverless-tier-overview?view=azuresql)

questions.explanation:
`VIEW DATABASE STATE` grants visibility into database-level state information, including the dynamic management information required to display database state and configuration properties in SSMS. `SHOWPLAN` is limited to query execution plans, `VIEW DEFINITION` exposes metadata definitions, and `SELECT` applies to data access.

You have four Azure subscriptions, each containing multiple Azure SQL databases.  
  
You need to update the column and index statistics for these databases. What should you use?

options.text: automatic tuning in Azure SQL Database

questions.explanation:
An Azure Automation runbook can run the required Transact-SQL maintenance, such as `sp_updatestats` or `UPDATE STATISTICS`, across Azure SQL databases in multiple subscriptions. Azure SQL Database statistics can be updated with these commands; automatic tuning manages plan correction and index recommendations, not general statistics-update jobs.\
\

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a database-backup solution for a SQL Server database running on an Azure virtual machine.  
  
If an Azure regional outage occurs, you must be able to restore the database backups. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
Which type of storage account should you use for the backups?
questions.explanation:
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) asynchronously replicates data to a geographically distant secondary Azure region, protecting backups from a primary-region outage. It is less expensive than read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS), whose additional secondary read access is not required merely to restore after failover.

**Learn more:** [Azure Storage redundancy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-redundancy) · [Change how a storage account is replicated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/redundancy-migration)

You enable columnstore archival compression.  
  
What are two possible outcomes of this configuration? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Queries that use the index will consume more disk I/O.

You have an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server 2019 instance that hosts a database named DB1.  
  
You have an Azure subscription containing an Azure SQL database named SQLDB1.  
  
You need to replicate DB1 to SQLDB1.  
  
Which replication type should you use?
questions.explanation:
Transactional replication supports an Azure SQL Database as a push subscriber from an on-premises SQL Server publisher. It initializes the subscriber with a snapshot and then propagates committed changes, maintaining the replicated copy. Peer-to-peer and merge replication are unsupported for Azure SQL Database subscribers; snapshot replication alone does not provide ongoing change replication.\
\
**Learn more:** [Replication to Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/replication-to-sql-database?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two Azure virtual machines, Server1 and Server2, that run Windows Server 2022 and are joined to an Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain named contoso.com.  
  
Both virtual machines have a default installation of Microsoft SQL Server 2019. Server1 is configured as a master server, and Server2 is configured as a target server.  
  
On Server1, you create a proxy account named contoso\sqlproxy.  
  
You need to make sure that SQL Server Agent job steps can be downloaded from Server1 and executed on Server2.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer provides part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: On Server2, grant the contoso\sqlproxy account the Impersonate a client after authentication user right.
On Server2, grant the contoso\sqlproxy account the Access this computer from the network user right.
On Server2, create a proxy account.
On Server1, set the AllowDownloadedJobsToMatchProxyName registry entry to 1.
On Server2, set the AllowDownloadedJobsToMatchProxyName registry entry to 1.

questions.explanation:
By default SQL Server Agent does not use proxy accounts for jobs that are downloaded from a master (MSX) server to a target (TSX) server. To enable this, two changes must be made on the target server (Server2). First, a proxy account with the SAME name as the master's proxy (contoso\sqlproxy) must be created on Server2, because downloaded job steps are matched by proxy name (choice C). Second, the AllowDownloadedJobsToMatchProxyName registry subkey under the SQL Server Agent hive on Server2 must be set to 1, since it defaults to 0 and otherwise the step fails with 'proxy matching is disabled on the target server' (choice E). The registry change on Server1 (D) is wrong because the setting only governs proxy matching on the target that executes the job.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Multiserver Jobs That Use Proxies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/ssms/agent/troubleshoot-multiserver-jobs-that-use-proxies) · [Make a Target Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ssms/agent/make-a-target-server)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL database called DB1.  
  
You must ensure that DB1 supports automatic failover with no data loss if a datacenter fails. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
Which deployment option and pricing tier should you configure?

options.text: Azure SQL Database managed instance General Purpose

questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Database Business Critical provides multiple synchronized replicas that can be distributed across availability zones. A zone failure triggers automatic failover to a fully synchronized replica, so committed data is not lost. Zone redundancy uses the existing Business Critical replicas and does not add a separate zone-redundancy cost, making it the least-cost option among the listed choices that meets the requirement.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An Azure subscription contains these resources:  
  
- 10 Azure SQL databases

You need to deploy a centralized monitoring solution for all Azure SQL resources while minimizing administrative effort.

You have an Azure SQL database named `db1` on a server named `server1`.  
  
The Intelligent Insights diagnostics log indicates that several tables have missing indexes.  
  
You need to make sure that indexes are created for those tables.  
  
What should you do?

questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Database automatic tuning includes the `CREATE_INDEX` option. When this option is enabled, Azure SQL Database automatically generates missing indexes and verifies their workload performance benefit. The setting is configured for the database through its automatic tuning settings.

You plan to implement a disaster recovery solution.  
  
You must be able to run disaster recovery drills on a regular basis. The solution must meet these requirements:  
  
- Minimize administrative effort for the recovery drills.  
- Isolate the recovery environment from the production environment.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Site Recovery supports test failovers for disaster-recovery drills without affecting ongoing replication or the production environment. The test failover can use an isolated, non-production network, and cleanup removes the test VMs after the drill, reducing operational effort.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that includes an Azure SQL database named DB1.  
  
You need to host elastic jobs by using DB1. DB1 will also be configured as a job target. The solution must support location-based Conditional Access policies.  
  
What should the elastic jobs use to access DB1?
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Elastic Jobs can use Microsoft Entra authentication through a user-assigned managed identity to connect to target databases. Microsoft Entra authentication enables Conditional Access controls, including location-based policies. System-assigned managed identities are not supported for Elastic Jobs, while SQL credentials and database-scoped credentials do not provide Microsoft Entra Conditional Access enforcement.

**Learn more:** [Elastic Jobs Overview - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/elastic-jobs-overview?view=azuresql) · [Microsoft Entra Authentication - Azure SQL Database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/authentication-aad-overview?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You receive many Azure Monitor alerts for an Azure SQL Database instance.  
  
You need to reduce the alert volume. You must receive alerts only when there is a significant change in usage patterns over an extended period.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer is part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Set the Alert logic threshold to Dynamic
Set the Alert logic threshold to Static

questions.explanation:
Dynamic thresholds use historical metric behavior to recognize anomalous patterns rather than comparing usage to a fixed value. Low threshold sensitivity permits greater deviation from the established pattern before an alert fires, reducing alert noise. Dynamic-threshold rules can also require violations across an evaluation period, which supports alerting only for sustained changes.

**Learn more:** [Alert rules with dynamic thresholds overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-dynamic-thresholds) · [Create Azure Monitor metric alert rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-create-metric-alert-rule)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a new Azure SQL database that contains a column storing confidential information.  
  
You must track every occasion when values from that column are returned by a query. The tracking information must be retained for 365 days from the date on which the query was run.  
  
Which three actions should you take? Each correct answer is part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Turn on auditing and write audit logs to an Azure Storage account.
Add extended properties to the column.
Turn on auditing and write audit logs to an Event Hub
Apply sensitivity labels named Highly Confidential to the column.
Turn on Azure Defender for SQL

questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Auditing writes audit events to Azure Storage and supports a retention period in days, so it can retain the records for 365 days. Applying a sensitivity label to the column lets the audit log include `data_sensitivity_information` identifying sensitivity classifications for data returned by queries. Azure Defender for SQL supplies the advanced SQL security and data-discovery/classification capability used in this sensitivity-based auditing solution.

**Learn more:** [Auditing for Azure SQL Database and Azure Synapse Analytics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/auditing-overview?view=azuresql) · [Data Discovery & Classification for Azure SQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/data-discovery-and-classification-overview?view=azuresql)

You discover that the plan cache is filled with compiled plans that were used only once.  
  
You run the `SELECT * FROM sys.database_scoped_configurations` Transact-SQL command and receive the results shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783791291665-tu58vfco.png)  
  
You need to relieve the memory pressure.  
  
What should you configure?
questions.explanation:
`OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS` reduces plan-cache memory use for many single-use ad hoc batches. When enabled, the database caches a small compiled-plan stub on the first compilation rather than the full compiled plan; a full plan is stored only if the batch is executed again. This prevents single-use plans from consuming the plan cache. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Microsoft SQL Server 2019 database named DB1 that uses the following database-level and instance-level features:  
  
- Clustered columnstore indexes  
- Automatic tuning  
- Change tracking  
- PolyBase  
  
You plan to migrate DB1 to an Azure SQL database.  
  
Which feature must be removed or replaced before DB1 can be migrated?
questions.explanation:
PolyBase is not supported in Azure SQL Database. Its functionality must be replaced, such as by using supported external-data access options where applicable. Clustered columnstore indexes, change tracking, and automatic tuning are supported in Azure SQL Database.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure SQL Managed Instance named SQLMI1 with the following configuration:

- Hardware generation: Standard-series (Gen5)  
  
You find that SQLMI1 is experiencing high memory pressure.  
  
You need to reduce the memory pressure on SQLMI1 while minimizing costs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Change Service tier to Business Critical.

questions.explanation:
Standard-series (Gen5) provides 5.1 GB of memory per vCore, while Premium-series provides 7 GB per vCore. Changing the hardware generation from Standard-series to Premium-series raises memory from 20.4 GB to 28 GB at the existing four-vCore size, avoiding the added cost of doubling the vCore count. Solution: You decrease the use of table variables and temporary tables.

questions.explanation:

Solution: You add more `tempdb` files.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
`2:3:905856` identifies a PFS page in `tempdb`, and `PAGELATCH_UP` on such a page indicates tempdb allocation contention. Adding `tempdb` data files distributes allocation activity among PFS pages, reducing latch contention and improving performance.\
\
**Learn more:** [Recommendations to reduce allocation contention in SQL Server tempdb database](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/sql/database-engine/performance/recommendations-reduce-allocation-contention) · [Diagnose and resolve latch contention on SQL Server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/diagnose-resolve-latch-contention?view=sql-server-ver16)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to implement the surrogate key for the retail store table. The solution must meet the requirements of the sales transaction dataset.  
  
What should you create?

options.text: a table that has a FOREIGN KEY constraint
a table the has an IDENTITY property

questions.explanation:
In Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools, a surrogate key is a column with a system-generated unique identifier that isn't derived from the source data. The IDENTITY property lets you implement this simply and efficiently: it automatically assigns an incrementing unique value to each new row and is designed to scale out across all distributions in a dedicated SQL pool without hurting load performance. This directly satisfies the retail store table's need for an automatically generated surrogate key while accommodating store address changes, without requiring the extra complexity of a shared SEQUENCE object, the referential-integrity purpose of a FOREIGN KEY constraint, or the historical row-versioning behavior of a system-versioned temporal table.

questions.explanation:

Your company's SLA requires that the database in the failover group become available as soon as possible if a major outage takes place.  
  
You configure the Read/Write failover policy as **Automatic**.  
  
Which two outcomes result from this configuration? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.

options.text: In the event of a datacenter or Azure regional outage, the databases will fail over automatically.
In the event of an outage, the databases in the primary instance will fail over immediately.
In the event of an outage, you can selectively fail over individual databases.
In the event of an outage, you can set a different grace period to fail over each database.
In the event of an outage, the minimum delay for the databases to fail over in the primary instance will be one hour.

questions.explanation:
With an Automatic (Microsoft-managed) failover policy, Azure SQL Managed Instance can automatically initiate failover for a disaster affecting the primary region. The service does not initiate automatic failover until the grace period has elapsed, and that grace period cannot be configured below one hour. Failover applies to the failover group rather than to individually selected databases.
